intro: Barmstedt is a small town in the district of Pinneberg, north of Hamburg, beside the Rantzauer See. By the road at the lake's car park stands a pedunculate oak that locals call the thousand-year oak. The district lists it as a natural monument and gives its age as about 600 to 650 years, its oldest. A reader sent us its photograph.
meta_description: The thousand-year oak of Barmstedt by the Rantzauer See: a 600-year-old natural monument north of Hamburg, where it stands and how to see it.
question_meta: The thousand-year oak of Barmstedt by the Rantzauer See: a 600-year-old natural monument north of Hamburg, where it stands and how to see it.
question_answer: The Thousand-Year Oak of Barmstedt stands beside the L 75 at the turn into the car park of the Rantzauer See. It is free to see at any hour.
question_context: People in Barmstedt call this pedunculate oak the Tausendjährige Eiche, the thousand-year oak. The district of Pinneberg, which has listed it as a natural monument since December 1997, gives a more careful age of about 600 to 650 years, and that still makes it the oldest natural monument in the district. It stands by the Landesstraße 75 where the road turns into the car park for the restaurant and playground on the Rantzauer See. A reader who sent us its photograph called it impressive even among the other oaks around the lake, partly hollow and knotted. The picture shows a massive grey trunk with a dark hollow at head height and three thick stems twisting apart into a wide crown. In 2011 the trunk measured 6.75 metres round at a metre above the ground. A wire mesh now guards the hollow, and the crown has been cut back to keep the old tree standing. It is beside a public road and car park, so it can be seen at any hour.

faq.q: Where is the thousand-year oak in Barmstedt?
faq.a: By the L 75 at the turn into the car park of the Rantzauer See, next to the lakeside restaurant and playground.

faq.q: How old is the Barmstedt oak really?
faq.a: The district of Pinneberg gives about 600 to 650 years. The thousand years is the local nickname.
Yes. It stands beside a public road and car park and can be seen at any hour, free.

trees.story:
In Barmstedt, north of Hamburg, people call this tree the Tausendjährige Eiche, the thousand-year oak. The district of Pinneberg is more modest. It has listed the pedunculate oak as a natural monument since December 1997 and gives its age as about 600 to 650 years, which still makes it the oldest natural monument in the district.

A reader sent us its photograph from the roadside by the Rantzauer See, where the oak stands at the turn into the car park for the lakeside restaurant and playground. "It is an impressive tree, even amongst the other oaks in the area," they wrote. "It is partially hollow [and] knotted."

The picture shows exactly that. From a massive grey trunk, open in a dark hollow at head height, three great stems climb and twist apart, carrying a crown still full of russet leaves in November. The trunk measured 6.75 metres round at a metre above the ground in 2011, and a wire mesh protects the hollow from further damage. The crown has been cut back over the years to keep the old tree standing.

Stand back across the road to take in the whole crown, then walk up close to see the hollow.
